psychological.label: Psychological Critic
psychological.reasoning: This axis is well grounded in scholarship on the Basil Hallward–Lord Henry Wotton dynamic. Critics repeatedly note Basil’s initial attraction to Henry’s wit and social brilliance alongside an early suspicion of his corrosive influence, and they also read Basil’s later confrontation with Henry as a moral repudiation of the corrupting force Henry exerts on Dorian. The arc from fascinated caution to ethical hostility is therefore a defensible relational reading of the novel.

citations.author: Murray, Nicholas

historical_cultural.label: Historical / Cultural Critic
historical_cultural.reasoning: This axis is well grounded in scholarship on the novel’s triangular structure: critics repeatedly note that Basil is initially drawn to Lord Henry’s brilliance while also sensing the danger of his influence, and that Basil later comes to regard Henry as morally corrosive and implicated in Dorian’s ruin. The claim is especially plausible if framed as a shift from fascination and caution to explicit ethical hostility, rather than as a simple friendship-to-enmity plot.

citations.relevance: Mighall discusses the Basil–Henry–Dorian triangle and Basil’s ambivalent response to Henry’s seductive cynicism, which supports the axis’s opening movement from fascination to caution.
